analysis.one_liner: Lets the Justice Department sue foreign oil cartels like OPEC for restricting oil supplies and raising U.S. prices.
analysis.headline: The bill to let the U.S. government sue OPEC over oil production cuts was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in March 2023 and never received a hearing or vote before the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: NOPEC would amend the Sherman Act, the main U.S. antitrust law, to make it illegal for foreign states like OPEC members to act together to limit oil production or set oil prices when that affects the U.S. market. It would strip away the usual defense that foreign governments cannot be sued in U.S. courts, and it would give the Attorney General alone the power to bring these cases. In effect, OPEC production cuts and price-fixing could be challenged in federal court.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. consumers, who pay the price when foreign oil cartels restrict supply and push up gasoline and heating costs. The bill also backs the U.S. antitrust system's core premise that cartels fixing prices can be hauled into court, and it would give the Justice Department a new tool against foreign price-setting that U.S. producers and refiners have no legal way to challenge today.
analysis.who_benefits_short: American consumers facing high gas prices

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a violation of U.S. antitrust law for any foreign state, agency, or agent to act collectively to limit oil production or distribution, set or maintain oil prices, or otherwise restrain trade in oil or natural gas when the action has a direct, substantial, and reasonably foreseeable effect on the U.S. market [S3].

Removes the two legal shields foreign states normally use in U.S. courts — sovereign immunity and the act of state doctrine — so an OPEC member could actually be sued and a judgment against it could be enforced against its property in the United States [S3].
Gives enforcement to the Attorney General, who could file suit in any federal district court under the normal antitrust rules, creating a practical remedy rather than a symbolic statement [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Foreign oil-producing states and their national oil companies, which would face antitrust lawsuits, damages, and potentially enforcement against their U.S. assets. Oil markets could also see retaliation risk: exporters whose coordination becomes a courtroom matter might respond by restricting supply, which would briefly raise prices for consumers — a cost an honest supporter of the bill has to acknowledge.
analysis.who_pays_short: OPEC states and their national oil companies

drawbacks.text: The bill strips foreign states of sovereign immunity for oil cartel claims and allows U.S. judgments to be enforced against their property [S3]. A genuine objection, acknowledged even by supporters, is that treating sovereign government policy as an antitrust violation in U.S. courts could invite retaliation from oil exporters and complicate U.S. relations with major suppliers — diplomacy normally handles OPEC disputes.
Enforcement rests solely with the Attorney General [S3]. That means no private lawsuits and no independent enforcement: if a future administration chooses not to challenge OPEC, the law sits unused.

The bill targets collective action 'to limit the production or distribution' of oil [S3]. Coordinated output decisions by sovereign nations are also legitimate economic and fiscal policy for those countries, and a court fight over them would raise hard separation-of-powers questions that the bill's narrow text does not resolve.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and broad: gasoline prices are set on a world market that OPEC openly manages through production quotas, and NOPEC would give the U.S. government a legal weapon against that conduct for the first time. The costs are real too — retaliation risk from exporters, a foreign-relations fight, and the fact that enforcement depends entirely on whoever is Attorney General. The bill is a narrow instrument aimed at a genuinely concentrated cartel, and its main flaw is not design but that it was never tested: no hearing, no mark-up, no vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it, and the bill died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Grassley introduced NOPEC on March 7, 2023, with three original cosponsors across both parties — Sens. Klobuchar, Lee, and Durbin [S1].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary [S5].
No further action appears in the record: no committee hearing, no markup, no floor vote, no House action. The bill sat in committee until the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: OPEC member states and other foreign oil exporters are better off: they faced no lawsuit, no change in the law, and no threat to their sovereign immunity from U.S. antitrust suits. Anyone who benefits from coordination among oil-exporting governments keeps the status quo.

for.name: Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Introduced NOPEC in the Senate on March 7, 2023

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (chaired by Dick Durbin, D-IL)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remaining 22 months of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: All four senators involved were bipartisan in pairings — a Republican lead sponsor with two Democratic cosponsors and one Republican — but the bill drew only three cosponsors total and never reached a floor vote, so no vote breakdown exists.

industries.note: These states coordinate production quotas and prices through OPEC, and NOPEC would make that conduct a violation of U.S. antitrust law subject to lawsuits and enforcement against their U.S. assets. Their profit from restricting supply comes directly out of what American consumers pay at the pump.

U.S. producers earn more when OPEC cuts keep world prices high; a legal tool that pressures exporters to pump more would push prices down and squeeze domestic producers' margins. Their interest in this bill runs against consumers', not with it.
